finding: There is no live range for this job on the site today (live is null), so nothing can be called too wide, too low or too high yet. Built totals for one set of front pads fitted, rotors reused (parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2015 Mazda3 about $89-$289 (0.4-1.0 hr); midsize 2015 Toyota Sienna about $132-$265 (0.8-1.0 hr); truck 2019 Chevrolet Silverado 1500 about $95-$381 (0.4-1.0 hr); luxury 2015 Acura RDX about $77-$270 (0.3-1.0 hr). Across the four classes that is roughly $77-$381. The public benchmarks for pads only sit at $148-$350 per axle (AAA $150-$350, Kelley Blue Book $150-$300, Jerry $148-$216), and the posted prices found start at about $159-$200 per axle. So the tops of our totals line up with the benchmarks, but the bottoms ($77-$132) are well below anything a shop posts: they pair an online aftermarket pad set ($36-$47) with a manufacturer warranty time. A realistic floor for a shop quote is about $150 per axle. How solid the labor times are: every low end is a manufacturer-stated time for the example vehicle itself, but they are not equally good. The Mazda 0.4 hr is a stand-alone 'front brake pads only' warranty operation, the best of the four. The Toyota 0.8 hr is a stand-alone pad operation for the Sienna, though the bulletin's parts list also includes two discs with no separate labor line. The GM 0.4 hr (Silverado) and the Acura 0.3 hr (RDX) are add-on lines, printed as extra time on top of another operation already being done, so they understate a pads-only visit; treat the truck and luxury low totals as too low. All four are warranty times, the bottom of what shops bill. The high ends all rest on 'about an hour per axle': AAA's general statement, a technician-run advice site's 1.0 hr for front pads on a 2019 Honda Odyssey (a comparable minivan for the midsize class, not the example vehicle), and for the truck a parts seller's 1-hour do-it-yourself estimate for the Silverado 1500 itself. None is a shop flat-rate book time for the example vehicle. One estimate site says 0.8-1.5 hours per axle; at 1.5 hr the tops would be about $369 (economy), $345 (midsize), $461 (truck) and $350 (luxury). None of the times used includes rotor resurfacing; Acura allows 0.9 hr for pads plus refinishing the discs on a later RDX, and several chains only sell pads together with resurfacing, which is one reason posted prices sit above our built totals. Confidence is medium by the rule used for these checks (every class has a stated time and two parts sources, and five of the eight hours figures are for the example vehicle), but two of the low ends are add-on lines and no class has a shop-level upper time for its own vehicle, so the totals are soft at both ends. Not found: a manufacturer pads-only time for the Ford F-150 or any stand-alone pads-only time for a full-size pickup (GM bulletins 24-NA-073 and 20-NA-020 name the operation but say only 'use published labor operation time'); a priced listing for the 2013-15 RDX pad set Acura's bulletin names (45022-TX4-A80, discontinued); a retailer part number for the Sienna pad set priced. Posted menu prices were found from only three sellers (one national chain's 'starting at' package, one chain coupon whose printed expiry has passed, and one dealer's stated range rather than a fixed price); other chain and dealer pages loaded showed only dollars-off coupons with no base price. Reviewer note (2026-11-20): GM's 0.4 hr and Acura's 0.3 hr are add-on lines, so they are cross-checks; the truck and luxury lows now use Mazda's stand-alone 0.4 hr (not the example vehicles). Luxury built total is now about $89-$270. Confidence is low: no class has a shop-level upper time for its own vehicle and two lows are not for the example vehicle. Posted pad prices were too few to show (one usable chain price, Pep Boys from $199.99 with resurfacing); the two others were an expired coupon and a dealer's stated range.
extras: Quotes often add: rotor resurfacing or new rotors (many shops will not fit pads to worn or scored rotors, and some chains only sell pads with resurfacing), a brake hardware or clip kit, pad-wear sensors on cars that have them, caliper service or replacement if a caliper is seized or leaking, a brake fluid exchange, shop supplies and disposal fees, an inspection or diagnosis fee, and sales tax. The rear axle is priced separately.
